rationale: Start with a broad mid-length scouting gradient at moderate temperature to observe the full elution window for all 6 compounds while reducing risk of truncation. This run should reveal whether peaks are unretained early, held to the final hold, or reasonably distributed across the gradient.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut retention time. The first and last peaks correspond roughly to phi_e about 0.15 and 0.54, so a narrower, steeper window with higher temperature should keep all peaks in-gradient while substantially shortening t_last.

We already have the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be made even faster while staying fully resolved. The current elution window suggests all peaks should still fit inside a slightly narrower, shorter, hotter gradient; this tests the margin on the limiting 1/2 and 4/5 pairs.

Push one more step faster and hotter to find the edge of full resolution. The limiting pair has shifted to peaks 1/2 and remains comfortably above 1.5, so this run tests whether further compression is still acceptable.

The last run crossed the resolution limit for the first pair, so back off by one step in gradient time while keeping the same hot, narrow window. This should restore R(1,2) above 1.5 and likely give a fully resolved method faster than injection 3.

At 60 C the narrower phi1=0.70 window compressed peaks 4/5 too much, so widen the upper end slightly while keeping the same short gradient. This should selectively relieve the late pair without giving back too much runtime.

At 60 C the limiting pair is now 4/5, and increasing phi1 from 0.70 to 0.75 improved it, so push one more step to 0.80 while keeping the short 8 min gradient. This tests whether the hotter method can recover full resolution and still beat the 50–55 C methods on runtime.

The 60 C, 8 min method is almost fully resolved, with only pair 4/5 just below threshold at R=1.48. Increasing phi1 one more step should slightly open the late pair while likely keeping all peaks under 10 minutes.

At 60 C the 8 min methods sit right on the edge, with the limiting pair switching between 1/2 and 4/5, so reduce temperature by one step at the best fast window. This should restore a comfortable resolution margin while keeping the run substantially shorter than the original 10 min, 50 C optimum.

With all pairs now comfortably resolved and the first peak still fairly early, raise phi0 one step to trim unneeded weak-mobile-phase time. This should shorten the run further while checking whether the early critical pair 1/2 remains above the 1.5 threshold.

The first peak remains retained enough at phi0=0.15 and the limiting pair 1/2 is still comfortably resolved, so raise phi0 another step to compress the early region further. This tests whether we can gain more speed without sacrificing the first-pair resolution.

phi0=0.20 pushed the first pair below threshold, so keep the successful phi0=0.15 but narrow the upper end one step to accelerate the late peaks. This should preserve the early-pair margin while testing whether full resolution is maintained with a slightly tighter gradient window.

The best fully resolved region is around phi0=0.15, phi1=0.80, T=55, so shorten tG from 8 to 6 min to locate the speed limit from that favorable window. This should show whether we can beat the 7.27 min last peak while keeping both critical pairs above 1.5.

The 6 min method is fully resolved but the first pair is now the limiting one at R=1.52, so one more shortening step will define whether we've reached the true edge. If it fails, injection 13 is likely near-optimal among tested conditions.

The 4 min gradient was too steep for the first pair, so stay at the successful 6 min length and test a slightly narrower upper window. This checks whether we can keep full resolution while trimming the late end relative to the current best fast method.

Injection 15 remained fully resolved with some margin on the critical first pair, so narrow the upper end one more step to see if the late peaks can be pulled in further. This explores whether a tighter 6 min window can improve speed without dropping below R=1.5.

The 6 min methods remain fully resolved and the first pair actually gains margin as phi1 narrows, so test one more step lower in phi1. This checks whether the late end can still be kept acceptably fast while preserving full resolution across all pairs.

The fastest fully resolved method so far is 0.15–0.80 in 6 min at 55 C, while 60 C mainly erodes the critical early pair. Testing 0.15–0.75 at 60 C may balance that by using a slightly narrower window to support the first pair while gaining a bit more speed.

The best fast region is clearly at 6 min and 55 C, with the first pair limiting; lowering phi0 should selectively improve that early-pair resolution. This run tests whether we can retain full resolution at 6 min while using a slightly more balanced window than the current 0.15-based methods.

A lower temperature may recover the early-pair selectivity lost at higher phi0, allowing a more aggressive starting composition without dropping below R=1.5. This probes whether phi0=0.20 can become viable at 6 min if we trade a small temperature decrease for better selectivity.

phi0=0.20 became viable at 50 C with good early-pair resolution, so increase phi1 one step to see whether the late region can be accelerated without harming the first pair. This may improve on the current 6.30 min last peak while staying fully resolved.

The 0.20–0.80, 6 min, 50 C method is fully resolved with some margin on the first pair, so raise phi0 one more step to trim the front of the run. This tests whether a slightly stronger start can further shorten retention without pushing the first pair below R=1.5.

phi0=0.25 was too aggressive for the first pair, so return to the successful phi0=0.20 and increase phi1 one step to accelerate the late end further. This is a targeted attempt to beat the current fastest fully resolved method while keeping early resolution above threshold.

The current fastest fully resolved method is 0.20–0.85 in 6 min at 50 C, and the limiting first pair still has a small safety margin. Increasing phi1 one more step is the most direct way to test for an additional reduction in t_last while likely remaining above R=1.5.

The current best method is still fully resolved with the limiting first pair at R=1.53, so one final increase of phi1 is the highest-value last test. This may deliver the shortest fully resolved run yet, while the remaining resolution margin suggests it has a plausible chance to stay at or above 1.5.
